content: The anti-inflammatory properties of omega-3 fatty acids, commonly found in fish oil, have been proposed as potentially beneficial for managing chronic inflammatory conditions, including inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effectiveness and safety of omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining remission in patients with Crohn's disease. To conduct this review, several databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, HealthSTAR, PubMed, and ACP Journal Club, were searched for relevant studies from their inception until November 2013. Only randomized, placebo-controlled trials (RCTs) were included. These studies had to involve patients of any age who were in remission at the time of recruitment and were followed for at least six months. The intervention under investigation was fish oil or omega-3 fatty acids administered in pre-defined dosages. Co-interventions were permitted only if they were equally distributed between the study groups. The primary outcome of interest was the relapse rate of Crohn's disease, while secondary outcomes included changes in disease activity scores, time to first relapse, and adverse events. Two independent investigators assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated study quality using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. The quality of evidence for the primary and selected secondary outcomes was reassessed using the GRADE system. Statistical analyses were performed using RevMan software, with risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and hazard ratios with 95% CI for time-to-event outcomes. Random-effects or fixed-effect models were applied based on the degree of heterogeneity, and sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. A total of six studies, involving 1,039 patients, met the inclusion criteria. The two largest studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias across all evaluated domains, while four studies had an unclear risk of bias regarding randomization and allocation concealment. Two studies were rated as having a high risk of bias due to incomplete outcome data and selective reporting. The results showed a marginally significant benefit of omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining remission. At 12 months, 39% of patients in the omega-3 group experienced a relapse, compared to 47% in the placebo group (6 studies, 1,039 patients; RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.98). However, a GRADE analysis rated the overall quality of evidence for this outcome as very low due to unexplained heterogeneity (I² = 58%), publication bias, and high or unclear risk of bias in four of the included studies. When only the two large, high-quality studies were considered, the benefit was no longer statistically significant. In this subgroup, 37% of patients in the omega-3 group relapsed at 12 months, compared to 42% in the placebo group (2 studies, 738 patients; RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.05). No significant heterogeneity was observed in this analysis (I² = 0%), and the GRADE analysis rated the quality of evidence as moderate due to limited data (294 events). No serious adverse events were reported in any of the studies. However, pooled analyses revealed a significantly higher incidence of diarrhea (4 studies, 862 patients; RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.84) and upper gastrointestinal symptoms (5 studies, 999 patients; RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.25 to 2.18) in the omega-3 treatment group. In conclusion, evidence from two large, high-quality studies suggests that omega-3 fatty acids are likely ineffective for maintaining remission in Crohn's disease. While omega-3 fatty acids appear to be safe overall, they may increase the risk of diarrhea and upper gastrointestinal symptoms.
